analogy.p: Imagine children on the edge of a merry-go-round spinning so fast they should be thrown off. If you only count the visible machinery, the grip does not seem strong enough, so you suspect there is an unseen mechanism holding them on. Dark matter is like that unseen extra grip, known only from its effect. For dark energy, picture a balloon that you expect to slow as it is inflated, yet it inflates faster and faster, so there must be an unseen source of extra push. The analogy breaks down because dark matter is spread through and around a galaxy rather than being a single hidden machine, and dark energy is not a pump pushing from outside.
analogy.t: A merry-go-round and a hidden crowd

bullets: **Dark matter** (sometimes called dark mass): matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation, so cannot be seen, but has gravity.
**Dark energy**: the name given to whatever is causing the expansion of the universe to speed up.
Both are used to explain observations that the Big Bang model with only visible matter cannot.
Neither has been directly detected, so they are **unconfirmed ideas** under active research.
Together they seem to make up most of the universe: ordinary matter is only about 5%.
Always answer with: observation, why it does not fit, the proposed explanation.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This is **physics-only** content within AQA Space physics. You need to know that scientists have found observations that the existing models cannot explain using only the visible matter, so they have proposed **dark matter** and **dark energy**. You are expected to say what each is and why scientists think it exists, but not to know a detailed mechanism, because scientists do not yet fully understand either. The key skill is explaining **why the idea was needed**: that is, what observation did not fit the existing model. Check your own copy of the specification for the exact wording used by your board, which may say 'dark mass'.

bullets: A bigger gravitational force is needed to keep an object in a faster orbit of the same radius.
Gravitational force decreases with distance, so the pull on outer stars should be smaller.
The expected graph of orbital speed against distance rises near the centre and then **falls** at large distances.
Visible mass means the stars, gas and dust that can be seen by their light.
These ideas link to the orbital motion topic: the speed must match the radius for a stable orbit.
The comparison between a prediction and a measurement is the heart of this topic.
core.h: Gravity and orbits: what we would expect
core.p: Stars in a galaxy orbit the centre of the galaxy because of the **gravitational attraction** of the matter inside their orbit. In the Solar System the Sun has almost all the mass, so planets that are further away feel a weaker pull and orbit **more slowly** (Mercury moves faster than Neptune). If most of a galaxy's mass is in its bright central region, the same rule should apply: stars far from the centre should orbit more slowly than those near the centre. Scientists made predictions from the visible mass and then measured the real speeds.

bullets: Observation: outer stars orbit at much the same speed as inner stars.
Expected: speeds should fall with distance if the visible matter is all there is.
Conclusion: there must be extra mass that we cannot see, spread through and beyond the galaxy in a **halo**.
The extra matter is called **dark matter** because it does not emit light.
The red-shift/Doppler method is used to measure speeds, linking this to the previous note.
Further evidence (an extension): light from distant objects is bent more than expected as it passes massive clusters, called gravitational lensing, which also indicates extra mass.
core.h: Evidence for dark matter: galaxy rotation
core.p: When astronomers measured the speeds of stars (using the Doppler effect on their light), they found that stars far from the centre orbit **just as fast** as those nearer to it, so the graph stays **flat** instead of falling. At those speeds the outer stars should fly off into space if only the visible mass were holding them in, because the visible matter provides too little gravitational pull. The simplest explanation is that there is a lot of **extra, unseen matter** around the galaxy providing additional gravity. This was shown convincingly by Vera Rubin and colleagues in the 1970s, and similar ideas were suggested earlier from the motion of galaxies in clusters.

bullets: It is not the same as black holes or dark clouds of ordinary gas, which can be detected in other ways.
It is called 'dark' because it does not emit or absorb light, not because it is the colour black.
Estimates suggest it makes up about 27% of the universe, around five times more than ordinary matter (approximate values).
It has not been directly detected, so it is an explanation that fits observations rather than a proven fact.
It would clump under gravity and form a halo around galaxies.
Some scientists propose changing the laws of gravity instead; this is a minority view and shows science considers alternatives.
core.h: What dark matter is (and is not)
core.p: Dark matter is **matter** that has **mass** and so produces gravity, but it does **not interact with electromagnetic radiation**: it does not give out, absorb or reflect light or any other part of the electromagnetic spectrum. That is why we cannot see it with any telescope and know it only through its **gravitational effects**. The nature of dark matter is unknown, and experiments, often deep underground, are looking for the particles that might make it up. So the correct phrase in an exam is that dark matter is **unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effect**.

bullets: Large distances mean looking back in time, because the light has taken billions of years to reach us.
If gravity slows the expansion, the early universe should have expanded faster than now.
Measuring distances needs a reliable 'standard candle', an object of known true brightness.
A **Type Ia supernova** is a very bright exploding white dwarf, with a very similar peak brightness each time (an extension fact), so it can be used to find distances.
Red-shift gives the recession speed and brightness gives the distance, so the two together show how the expansion has changed.
This is the experiment that gave the surprising result.
core.h: Recap: the expansion and what was expected
core.p: From the previous note, observations of red-shift show that the universe is **expanding** and the Big Bang model explains this. Gravity pulls all matter together, so scientists expected that gravity would **slow down** the expansion over time, just as a ball thrown upwards slows down. They set out to measure how much the expansion had slowed, which means measuring the expansion in the distant past (looking at very distant galaxies) and comparing it with today's rate.

bullets: Observation: distant galaxies are moving away **faster and faster**; the expansion of the universe is accelerating.
Expected from gravity: the expansion should slow down.
Proposed explanation: **dark energy**, some form of energy that acts against gravity on the largest scales.
Brightness of a supernova decreases with the square of its distance, so a dim supernova means a larger distance (inverse square law, an extension).
The discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011.
Dark energy is thought to be about 68% of the universe, but its nature is a major unsolved problem.
core.h: Evidence for dark energy: the accelerating expansion
core.p: In **1998**, two teams studying distant supernovae found that the supernovae were **fainter than expected**, so they were **further away** than they should have been if the expansion had been slowing. The only way this happens is if the expansion of the universe has been **speeding up** (accelerating). Observations since then show that the **distant galaxies are receding ever faster**. Gravity alone would slow the expansion, so something else must be pushing space apart. That unknown cause is called **dark energy**.

bullets: **Dark matter**: explains the high orbital speeds of stars in galaxies (and the motion of galaxies in clusters); its effect is extra gravitational attraction.
**Dark energy**: explains the accelerating expansion of the universe seen in distant supernovae; its effect is repulsive, speeding up expansion.
Dark matter is thought of as matter with mass; dark energy is a property or energy of space itself and is not made of particles in the same way.
Both are 'dark' because they cannot be seen directly, and both are known only through their effects.
Both are open research problems with no direct detection yet.
Dark matter is about 27% and dark energy about 68% of the universe, so ordinary matter, which includes all the stars and us, is only about 5%.
core.h: Comparing dark matter and dark energy
core.p: Students often mix up the two. The names are similar, but they explain **different observations** and have **opposite effects**. Dark matter is an extra source of **gravity** that holds galaxies together, so it pulls things in. Dark energy is a cause of **expansion** and pushes space apart on the largest scales. A good approach is to remember what each one explains.

bullets: Step 1: observation that does not fit the current model.
Step 2: new hypothesis that could explain it.
Step 3: testing by further observation and experiment.
Step 4: peer review and repeat by other scientists.
Step 5: model is accepted, modified or replaced depending on the evidence.
Say 'suggests' and 'is thought to be', and avoid claiming that dark matter or dark energy has been proven.
core.p: These topics are good examples of **how scientific models develop**. A model (such as the Big Bang with only visible matter) is tested against observations. When the observations do not fit, scientists do not ignore them: they **propose new ideas** (dark matter, dark energy), make predictions, and design new experiments. The new idea is accepted only when it is supported by more independent evidence. Dark matter and dark energy are currently **hypotheses with supporting evidence**, not established, directly observed facts.

bullets: Red-shift: used to measure speeds of galaxies and stars (Doppler effect).
Gravity and orbits: the circular orbit needs a centripetal force provided by gravity.
Stars: the visible matter that we can see is made of stars, gas and dust; this is the matter we can observe.
Waves: electromagnetic radiation is how all visible information reaches us, and dark matter does not interact with it.
Scientific method: evidence, hypothesis, testing and peer review.
Maths skills: ratios and percentages of the universe and the inverse-square relationship.
core.h: Link to the Big Bang model and other topics
core.p: Dark matter and dark energy extend the Big Bang model rather than replacing it. The model still says the universe began from a small, hot, dense state and has expanded, but a full description needs the dark components. Linking with other parts of physics shows depth of understanding.

bullets: Dark energy: 'distant galaxies are accelerating away from us, whereas gravity would slow the expansion, so another cause, dark energy, is proposed.'
State that neither can be seen or directly detected and are known from their effects.
Use phrases: 'cannot be detected directly', 'inferred from', 'gravitational effect', 'accelerating expansion'.
Conclude: 'these are current explanations, and more evidence is needed.'
In a six mark question, include both ideas, the evidence for each, and a statement about uncertainty.
core.h: A model answer chain for exam questions
core.p: To score highly, structure answers by the **observation, expectation, explanation** pattern. Each statement should carry a reason, which is what separates a top grade answer from a list of facts. Dark matter: 'stars at the edge of galaxies orbit faster than expected from the visible mass, so there must be extra unseen mass providing more gravity.'.

bullets: Describe: speed increases near the centre, then stays roughly **constant** at large distances.
Compare: from the visible matter alone the speed would **decrease** at large distances.
Use data: quote a speed and a distance read from the graph, with units (km/s and kpc).
Conclude: there must be **additional mass** that cannot be seen, providing extra gravitational pull.
Name it: this unseen mass is called **dark matter**, spread in a halo around the galaxy.
Avoid saying the stars are 'pulled outwards' by dark matter: the extra gravity pulls them **inwards**, keeping them in orbit.
A flat curve means the mass inside each orbit keeps increasing with distance, even where little light is seen.
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph of orbital speed against distance from the centre of a galaxy. You should **describe the shape** first (rises, then stays roughly constant), then **compare it with the prediction** from the visible matter (rises, then falls), and finally **state what the difference suggests**: more mass than can be seen. Quote values from the graph, such as the speed and the distance where the curve levels off, because a numerical comparison gains a mark that a vague description does not. The speeds themselves are found from the Doppler shift of starlight.

bullets: Same true brightness but dimmer appearance means **greater distance**.
Brightness is proportional to 1 ÷ distance², so if a source looks 4 times dimmer it is 2 times further away (extension).
The red-shift of the host galaxy tells you how fast it is moving away.
Combining distance (how far back in time we look) and speed shows how the expansion rate has **changed over time**.
Result: expansion was slowing earlier on, then began to **accelerate**.
Dark energy is the **name** for the cause, not an explanation of what it is.
The 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for this discovery.
core.h: Standard candles and the supernova evidence in detail
core.p: To find how far away a distant galaxy is, astronomers use objects of **known true brightness** called standard candles. A **Type Ia supernova** is an extension example: its peak brightness is very similar each time, so how bright it **looks** tells you how far away it is, because light spreads out and the apparent brightness falls as the **square of the distance**. In 1998 the observed supernovae were fainter, so further away, than expected for a slowing expansion. This showed that the expansion has been speeding up, and the unknown cause is named dark energy.

exam: Always give the **observation** first, then the **reason it does not fit**, then the **proposed explanation**.
1 mark: a definition such as 'matter that cannot be seen because it does not emit light' or 'the cause of the accelerating expansion'.
2 marks: a fact plus a reason, for example 'stars at the edge orbit faster than expected, so extra mass is present'.
4 marks: describe the observation, say what was expected, explain what is proposed and say why it is named 'dark'.
6 marks: cover both dark matter and dark energy with their evidence, and comment on the uncertainty because neither has been detected directly.
Use phrases: 'cannot be detected directly', 'only inferred from its gravitational effect', 'expansion is accelerating'.
Do not say 'proved'; say 'suggests' or 'is thought to'.
Rotation curve graphs: describe the shape (rises then flat), compare with the predicted shape (rises then falls), then explain the difference.
Data questions: quote values from the table or graph, with units, in the comparison.
If asked to evaluate: the evidence is consistent but indirect, and the nature of both is unknown.

mistakes.r: Dark matter is unseen matter inferred from its gravity. Black holes are collapsed stars that can be detected in other ways.
mistakes.w: Dark matter is the same as black holes.

mistakes.r: It is 'dark' because it does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation, so cannot be seen.
mistakes.w: Dark matter is matter that is black in colour.

mistakes.r: Dark energy is the proposed cause of the accelerating expansion, so it pushes the universe apart. Dark matter provides extra gravity.
They have not been directly detected. They are explanations for observations and are still being researched.
mistakes.w: Scientists have found dark matter and dark energy.

mistakes.r: They are observed to orbit as fast as inner stars, which is the problem that dark matter explains.
mistakes.w: Stars at the edge of galaxies orbit more slowly because gravity is weaker.

mistakes.r: Observations since 1998 show the expansion is accelerating, which is why dark energy was proposed.
mistakes.w: The expansion of the universe is slowing down because of gravity.

mistakes.r: They explain different observations and have opposite effects: dark matter adds gravity, dark energy drives expansion.
mistakes.w: Dark matter and dark energy are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Ordinary matter is only about 5%, whereas dark matter is about 27% and dark energy about 68% (approximate).
mistakes.w: Dark matter is a tiny part of the universe.

summary: The specification asks you to explain why scientists have proposed dark matter (unseen matter whose extra gravity explains the fast orbits of stars in galaxies) and dark energy (the unknown cause of the accelerating expansion of the universe seen in distant supernovae), and to say that neither has yet been directly detected. It matters because it shows how models change when observations do not fit, and is a typical 'explain the evidence' exam question.

terms.d: Matter that does not emit, absorb or reflect electromagnetic radiation, detected only through its gravitational effects.
Another name for dark matter used in some specifications.
The name given to the unknown cause of the accelerating expansion of the universe.
A graph of the orbital speed of stars in a galaxy against their distance from the galaxy's centre.
A large, roughly spherical region around a galaxy, thought to contain dark matter.
Ordinary matter (stars, gas and dust) that emits, absorbs or reflects electromagnetic radiation and can be observed.
The observation that distant galaxies are receding at an increasing speed, so the universe's expansion is speeding up.
The explosion of a star at the end of its life, which can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.
An astronomical object of known true brightness, used to calculate its distance from how bright it appears.
The force of attraction between all objects with mass, larger for greater mass and smaller for greater distance.
The path of an object around another, held in place by gravitational force.
An increase in the observed wavelength of light from a source moving away from the observer.
The model that the universe began from a very small, hot, dense region about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding since.
A proposed explanation that can be tested by further observation or experiment.
Evaluation of scientific work by other independent scientists before it is accepted.
The bending of light from a distant object by the gravity of massive matter between it and the observer (extension).

worked.ans: Stars at the edges of galaxies orbit faster than the visible matter can explain. Extra mass that cannot be seen (dark matter) must be providing additional gravitational force to keep them in orbit.
worked.q: Explain why scientists have suggested that dark matter exists. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: stars in galaxies orbit the centre because of gravitational attraction.
Mark 2: from the visible matter, stars further out should orbit more slowly.
Mark 3: stars at the edge of galaxies are observed to orbit as fast as inner stars.
Mark 4: so there must be extra unseen mass providing more gravity, which is called dark matter.

worked.ans: The speed remains at about 200 km/s instead of decreasing, which suggests extra unseen mass (dark matter) in a halo around the galaxy.
worked.q: A graph of orbital speed against distance from the centre of a galaxy shows the speed rising to 200 km/s at 8 kpc and then staying at about 200 km/s out to 20 kpc. Describe how this differs from what is predicted from the visible matter and explain what it suggests. (3 marks)
steps: Prediction: speed should rise then fall as distance increases beyond the visible matter.
Observation: speed stays constant at about 200 km/s between 8 kpc and 20 kpc.
Explanation: more mass than visible must be present at larger distances, providing extra gravity.

worked.ans: P is 2 times further away than Q. Supernovae were further than expected, so the expansion is accelerating, which is attributed to dark energy.
worked.q: Two Type Ia supernovae have the same true brightness. Supernova P appears 4 times dimmer than supernova Q. Assuming brightness is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, how many times further away is P? Explain why dim distant supernovae led to the idea of dark energy. (4 marks)
steps: Brightness is proportional to 1 / d squared, so d is proportional to 1 / square root of brightness.
P is 4 times dimmer: distance ratio = square root of 4 = 2.
Distant supernovae in 1998 were dimmer, so further, than expected for a slowing expansion.
So the expansion has been accelerating, and the cause is called dark energy.
